blocks.text: We now come again to a group of birds about which the commentaries and lexicographers give not the slightest information, and for which we are therefore once more reduced to attempting conjectures. Perhaps we shall succeed in at least offering a few guiding hints.
The Bullfinch.

Chulin 141b mentions a clean bird חימה. Also reads: חמאה. Here we have only to seek out the basic meaning of the root of that word. חימה means, first, wonderful, perfect, and one might think of the wonderful bird of paradise, which Scaliger (see Göthe and Zelter, Briefwechsel vol. 6, p. 96) calls Monstrum sine vitio; but this splendid bird belongs to the raven family and cannot count as a clean bird.
Secondly, חמאה means garlic, and, as is well known, larks, because they eat field garlic, have its pleasant taste;
[p. 182] but this reason is far too weak for thinking, on that account, of the lark in our passage (which in any case has a different name, see §. 214).

Thirdly, תם means simple, and so the stupid, guileless and incautious bullfinch may be meant here. Its simplicity has become proverbial; it belongs to the sparrow family and can therefore rightly have been regarded as a clean bird.

In the Midrasch Rabba (Schir ha-Schirim) the word תמתי, used of the dove, is rendered once (fol. 12, col. d) as beautiful and the second time (ibid. fol. 17, col. d beginning) as perfect; but the dove cannot be meant in our Talmud passage, since the Talmud never calls this bird תמתי.
The Penguin.

Chulin 62b mentions two birds: the בוניא is permitted to be eaten, the פרוא is forbidden to be eaten. There must be an essential contrast here in the nature of the two birds, and I believe I find it in the fact that פרוא is a lean bird (see the following article), and בוניא a fat one. Here we speak of the latter. Aruch reads כניא, which means fat. The fatty mesentery of cattle is called כנחא, which Münster (in the Lex.) explains as Sumen pinguendo intestinorum; I would therefore understand by בוניא the penguin (Spheniscus demersus; Voigt l. c. 2, p. 422). As a goose it may rightly have been declared clean. But our reading too could speak for our explanation, for while פרוא is the Avis prava, the lean bird, בוניא is the Avis bona, the good, i.e., fat bird; thus the quail, because of its fatness, is called in Arabic سَمَانِي [samānī], Samana (Rosenmüller loc. cit. p. 346).
The Sea Gull.

Like בוניא (§. 222), פרוא (Chulin 62b) is also a water bird, and in the latter name I suspect the very lean sea gull. The Hebrew שחף (Lev. 11, 16) is explained by most commentaries and lexicographers as gull, from שחף "emaciated", "lean", and this is quite especially the sea gull (Larus marinus [p. 183] in L.). The Talmudic פרוא may be formed from the Latin prava, "bad"; cf. the Judeo-German parva, by which one understands something re-melted, which is probably corrupted from prava. Cf. §. 378.
The Storm Gull.

Chulin 102b an unclean bird is called קלניתא, which Raschi explains as עוף כחוש מאוד "very lean bird"; the Greek Κηλὸν [kēlon] also means lean, dry, and so קלניתא, like פרוא (§. 223), may be a gull, namely the smallest species, the storm gull. This gull has many feathers but very little flesh, and is rightly the bird whose limbs (אבר), as our passage says, are not the size of an olive (כזית).

On B. batra 20a Raschi says: the קלניתא is so lean that no one eats it. In this passage it is also said that one may put the קלניתא into a child's hands, because it does not scratch; as is well known, all gulls can easily be kept as cage birds (Voigt l. c. 2, p. 388). On children playing with birds kept in the house see Job. 40, 29.
The Skua.

B. batra 20a, where the storm gull (§. 224) is discussed, mentions a bird that is כעין קלניתא "like the קלניתא", i.e., which is lean like the storm gull but not so peaceable; one does not put it into a child's hands, because it scratches. The skua cannot be kept as a cage bird, for it is particularly wild and rapacious.
The Bird of Paradise.

Berachoth 6b it says: In the coastal cities (כרכי ים) there is a bird called כרום which casts many colors at sunrise. There is no doubt that כרום is formed from Χρῶμα [chrōma], color, just as the Midrasch Rabba (Bereschit fol. 9, col. 2) calls a bird endowed with 365 colors צבוע "colored one" [p. 184] *). In our Talmud passage a bird must be named whose metallic-colored plumage shimmers variously in the sunlight, and that will probably be our splendid bird. The Spaniards call it Pajaro del sol (or Passaros de sol), sun bird, and indeed one believes one sees a shining ball of fire when the bird of paradise floats along in the air. It lives in the farthest East Indies, especially on New Guinea and the other Papuan islands, and was therefore known to seafarers, to which our passage alludes.
The Pelican.

Chulin 63a names four birds whose names were evidently formed from their shape. The first is called לקני and is permitted to be eaten. Apart from the fact that the word may perhaps have arisen from Πελεκὰν [pelekan] by dropping the first syllable, לקן also means "jug", "vessel", which is in a certain sense what the pouch stretching beneath the beak serves as. In this pouch, or cellular tissue, the bird holds the food it has taken in, which it then lets the young fetch from its throat; it thus has a vessel in which it keeps the food.
Cf. Appendix s.v. אם הים
